title: Thanks for the King's Victory
overview: The people thank God for answering their king's prayers with victory and long life, then look ahead with confidence that his enemies will fall.

parts.label: Prayer answered (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The king is glad, but the song says his joy comes from God's strength rather than his own army. It reads like the answer to the previous psalm, where the people prayed that God would grant the king his heart's desire before battle.

parts.label: Crown, life and honor (vv. 3-6)
parts.note: God is pictured coming out to meet the king with gifts and a gold crown, an image of the highest royal success. The line about life "for ever and ever" echoes God's promise of a lasting royal family, and Christians have also read it as pointing to Jesus.

parts.label: The heart of it (v. 7)
parts.note: This middle verse gives the reason for everything else: the king trusts the LORD. He stands firm because of God's faithful love, not his own merit.

parts.label: The enemies' defeat (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: It is unclear whether "you" here means God or the king acting for God, since verse 9 suddenly speaks of the LORD as "he." The images are harsh, with enemies burned as in a furnace and their children wiped out, reflecting ancient wars where a rival family line was ended so it could never rise again.

parts.label: Closing praise (v. 13)
parts.note: The song ends by turning all the credit back to God. The people promise to sing about his power.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether this psalm is mainly about a historical king of Israel, later applied to Jesus, or was meant from the start as a prophecy of him.
think: When a leader credits their success to something greater than themselves, does that make them easier or harder to trust?
